deep.reconstruction:
Context. The previous page is headed 'Astralgeometrie', the term Schweikart used for the non-Euclidean (hyperbolic) geometry. There Gauss gives the volume of a thin prism-like body of infinitesimal height Aa as (1/2)·Aa·BC·sin(i·AD)/i. Since sin(i·u)/i = sinh u, this is the hyperbolic replacement of the Euclidean factor AD. Gauss is working with spherical-type formulas and passing to the 'astral' case by imaginary substitution. This page, headed 'Noch zierlicher' ('even more elegant'), gives a second volume element of the same kind.

Setup (from figure and text).
- ABC is a triangle with a right angle at B and angle φ at A.
- AB = x (the leg) and AC = r (the hypotenuse).
- D lies close to C, so ABD is a congruent right triangle (BD ⊥ AB). It is obtained by turning ABC about the edge AB through an infinitely small dihedral angle θ.
- The 'Pyramide ABCD' is the resulting thin tetrahedron, a wedge at edge AB. To first order in θ its volume equals that of the wedge swept out by triangle ABC rotating about AB through θ.
- Claim: Volume = (1/2)(x − r cos φ)·θ.

Reconstruction (my steps). Use coordinates about the axis AB: z = distance along AB from A, ρ = distance from the axis, ψ = rotation angle.

Spherical space of curvature +1:
- Metric: ds² = dρ² + sin²ρ dψ² + cos²ρ dz², so dV = sinρ cosρ dρ dψ dz.
- Hence V = θ ∫_0^x ∫_0^{ρ(z)} sinρ cosρ dρ dz = (θ/2) ∫_0^x sin²ρ(z) dz.
- Parametrize the hypotenuse by s = AP. The right triangle APQ gives sin ρ = sin s sin φ and tan z = cos φ tan s.
- Then dz = cos φ ds / (1 − sin²φ sin²s).
- Integrand: sin²ρ dz = cos φ [1/(1 − sin²φ sin²s) − 1] ds.
- The first part integrates over 0..r to ∫ dz = x; the second gives r cos φ.
- So V = (θ/2)(x − r cos φ), exactly Gauss's formula.

Hyperbolic space of curvature −1:
- dV = sinhρ coshρ, with sinh ρ = sinh s sin φ and tanh z = cos φ tanh s.
- The same computation gives V = (θ/2)(r cos φ − x), and here r cos φ > x.
- Equivalently, with radius R: V = (R²θ/2)(x − r cos φ). Putting R = ik turns this into (k²θ/2)(r cos φ − x).

Euclidean check: x = r cos φ, so the bracket vanishes to first order. The leading term of the expansion is θ r³ cos φ sin²φ / 6. This equals the Euclidean wedge of the cone, (θ/2π)(π/3)(x tan φ)² x.

What it serves: an elementary volume element for building up volumes of tetrahedra and solids in non-Euclidean space. It is in effect the derivative of the volume of the solid of revolution with respect to the rotation angle, and a special case of the Schläfli-type relation between volume, edge lengths and dihedral angles.
errors: The formula (1/2)(x − r cos φ)θ is exactly right for spherical space of unit radius (more generally R²θ/2·(x − r cos φ)).
In hyperbolic space of curvature −1, x < r cos φ, so read literally the expression is negative; the correct value is (θ/2)(r cos φ − x).

This sign is consistent only if one adopts Gauss's evident convention of computing spherically and substituting an imaginary radius (factor R² = −k²). The constant factor and its sign are not stated on the page.
'Pyramide ABCD' (a tetrahedron) is identified with the rotational wedge. This is valid only to first order in the infinitesimal θ; that is acceptable given 'unendlich klein'.

results.what: Volume of the infinitesimal wedge (tetrahedron ABCD) obtained by rotating a right triangle (leg AB = x, hypotenuse AC = r, angle φ at A) about AB through dθ: V = (1/2)(x − r cos φ) dθ in spherical/'astral' form (hyperbolic: (1/2)(r cos φ − x) dθ).
results.modern_name: Volume element of a solid of revolution in constant-curvature space; special case of the Schläfli differential volume formula (dV = −(1/2)Σ ℓ dα for curvature −1, (1/2)Σ ℓ dα for +1).
results.usually_credited_to: Hyperbolic volumes of solids: Lobachevsky (1829–1836) and J. Bolyai (1832). The general differential volume formula: Schläfli (1850s, published 1858/60).

results.what: Use of sin(i·u)/i (= sinh u) to pass from spherical to hyperbolic ('Astral') formulas.
results.modern_name: Imaginary-radius correspondence between spherical and hyperbolic geometry.
results.usually_credited_to: Lambert (1766, hint), Taurinus (1826), Lobachevsky; Gauss's use is known from his correspondence and Nachlass.

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss's interest in non-Euclidean volumes (e.g. the tetrahedron problem he mentions to W. Bolyai in 1832) and his imaginary-radius method are known. A clean closed-form volume element for a rotational wedge, essentially a Schläfli-type relation, is a notable unpublished technical detail but not a major priority claim. Lobachevsky had comparable volume computations, and parts of Gauss's Astralgeometrie notes appear in Werke VIII.

checkable.asserts: Spherical case: dz/ds = cos φ/(1 − sin²φ sin²s) when tan z = cos φ tan s (result 0).
Spherical integrand sin²ρ dz/ds splits as cos φ/(1 − sin²φ sin²s) − cos φ, so ∫_0^r = x − r cos φ (result 0).
Hyperbolic case: dz/ds = cos φ/(1 + sin²φ sinh²s) when tanh z = cos φ tanh s (result 0).
Hyperbolic integrand splits as cos φ − dz/ds, giving V = (θ/2)(r cos φ − x) (result 0).
Leading term is r³ cos φ sin²φ/3, so (θ/2)(r cos φ − x) ≈ θ r³ cos φ sin²φ/6, the Euclidean cone wedge.
Spherical: x − r cos φ ≈ r³ cos φ sin²φ/3 > 0, consistent with Gauss's sign.
sin(i u)/i = sinh u, the substitution used on the previous page (result 0).

transcription_corrections: Line 'Inhalt der [-unend-] Pyramide ABCD': the article reads more like 'des' (Gauss's slip for 'der'); the crossed-out word is 'unend' (start of 'unendlich').
The figure: the dotted line runs from A to D along/near AC; C and D are almost coincident at the right end, D slightly below C, indicating the infinitesimal rotation.
